Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 84, verses 1–6:

[218] ﴿When the sky splits open,﴾ ﴿and listens to its Lord, and it is worthy of that;﴾ ﴿and when the earth is stretched out,﴾ ﴿and casts out what is within it and empties itself,﴾ ﴿and listens to its Lord, and it is worthy of that;﴾ ﴿O man, you are toiling towards your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him.﴾

The adverbial phrase ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ (idha al-sama'u inshaqqat, "when the sky splits open") is placed before its governing verb, "kadih" (toiling), for the sake of awe-inspiring emphasis and to create suspense before the predicate. The original order of the speech in consideration is: "O man, you are toiling, when the sky splits open, etc."

However, since "idha" is attached to a part of the clause ﴿إنَّكَ كادِحٌ﴾ (innaka kadih, "you are toiling"), and since "idha" is an adverb carrying the meaning of a conditional, the sentence becomes: "O man, you are toiling" as the answer to the condition of "idha." Accordingly, they say that "idha" is an adverb that governs (khafid) its condition and is governed in the accusative (mansub) by its answer. That is, it governs the clause of its condition by being prefixed to it, and it is in the accusative by its answer, because it is connected to it. Thus both are governing and governed, according to the difference of perspective.

"Idha" is an adverb of future time, and the verb in the clause annexed to "idha" is interpreted as future, yet it is expressed in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, because the basic meaning of "idha" is the certainty of the condition's occurrence.

"Inshaqqat" is the intransitive (mutawi') form of "shaqqaha," meaning: when a splitter splits the sky, it splits; that is, God wills its splitting and it splits, as indicated by His following words, "and listens to its Lord."

"Al-inshiqaq" (splitting) here is the same as "al-infitar" mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْفَطَرَتْ﴾ (Surah al-Infitar 82:1). It is a splitting that appears to people in the atmosphere of the sky, due to a disruption in the composition of the air sphere, or due to the appearance of celestial bodies that leave their usual orbits in the upper atmosphere, so the air dome splits. It is thus a splitting that occurs when the order of this world is disrupted.

The subject is placed before the predicate verb in ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ rather than saying "idha inshaqqat al-sama'" in order to convey the strengthening of the judgment, which is the conditional suspension; that is, this condition is certain to occur, in addition to what the conditional "idha" implies of intending certainty of the occurrence of the condition, unlike "inna."

"Adhinat" means "istama'at" (listened). The verb "adhina" is derived from a fixed noun, which is the noun "udhun" (with a dammah on the hamza), the organ of hearing in a human. One says "udhun lahu," just as one says "istama' lahu," meaning he gave his ear to him.

[219] Here it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) in the sense of being affected: by God's creative command that it should split. It is not a metaphorical extension (isti'arah tab'iyyah) nor a representative metaphor (tamthiliyyah).

The expression "Rabbiha" (its Lord) is used instead of other divine names and ways of designating Him, because of what the description of the Lord implies of sovereignty and governance.

The clause "wa huqqat" is a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined clause and the clause it is conjoined to.

The meaning is: it is worthy of listening to its Lord, because it does not go outside the authority of His power, however great its thickness, however firm its creation, and however long the time of its sealing. All of that is only by God's decree for it; He is the one who, when He wills, removes it.

The object of "huqqat" is omitted, indicated by the verb "adhinat li-rabbiha," i.e., "and it is worthy of that submission and being affected." One says "huqqa fulanun bi-kadha," meaning a right was directed toward him. Since the agent of directing the right is generally not clear, the verb "huqqa bi-kadha" is used in the passive in usage, and its subject has the sense of the passive participle. So one says "haqiqun 'alayhi kadha" as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿حَقِيقٌ عَلى أنْ لا أقُولَ عَلى اللَّهِ إلّا الحَقَّ﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:105), and "huwa mahquq bi-kadha." Al-A'sha said:

"Indeed, you are worthy that you respond to his voice, and that you know that the one who is helped is successful."

The discussion of the clause ﴿وإذا الأرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾ (wa idha al-ardu muddat) is like the discussion of the clause ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ in placing the subject before the predicate verb.

"Madd al-ard" means spreading it out. The apparent meaning of this is that what is upon it of mountains is removed, as hide is stretched, so its folds disappear, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ فَقُلْ يَنْسِفُها رَبِّي نَسْفًا فَيَذَرُها قاعًا صَفْصَفًا لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا ولا أمْتًا﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha 20:105).

[220] Among the meanings of "madd" is that it results from the expansion of the extent of its surface, by its cracking through earthquakes and the emergence of parts of its interior to its surface.

Among the meanings of "madd" is that its sphericity is removed by the stretching of its body until it becomes elongated after being round. All of that indicates the disruption of the order of the earth's movement and the change of the conditions of gravity and of the air sphere around the earth, and this is followed by the cessation of this world.

His words ﴿وألْقَتْ ما فِيها﴾ (and it casts out what is within it) are suitable to be understood in accordance with what fits these possibilities regarding the stretching of the earth, and they admit of the meaning that other parts are ejected from the interior of the earth, whose ejection has an effect in destroying existing things, such as volcanoes, the eruption of huge rocks, and the bursting forth of springs onto the surface of the earth, so that there is a flood.

"Takhallat" means it brought out what was in its interior so that nothing of it remained; because the verb "takhalla" indicates the intensity of emptying oneself of something, due to what the morphological pattern "tafa''ala" conveys of the sense of effort in the act, as one says "takarrama fulanun" when he exaggerated in generosity.

The meaning is: nothing remains of what is in the interior of the earth, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿وأخْرَجَتِ الأرْضُ أثْقالَها﴾ (Surah al-Zalzalah 99:2).

The discussion of the parallel of His words "wa adhinat li-rabbiha wa huqqat" has been mentioned above.

The clause ﴿يا أيُّها الإنْسانُ إنَّكَ كادِحٌ﴾ up to its end is the answer to "idha," in view of what is derived from it, namely His words "fa-mulaqihi." This was attributed to al-Mubarrad, meaning: because the last conjoined clause with "fa" in the reports is the one intended, of what was mentioned together with it.

So the meaning is: when the sky splits open and when the earth is stretched out, you will meet your Lord, O man, after your toil toward meeting Him. Thus His words ﴿إنَّكَ كادِحٌ﴾ are an interjected insertion placed before the intended point, like a parenthetical remark.

Al-Mubarrad also permitted that the answer to "idha" be omitted, indicated by His words "fa-mulaqihi," and the estimate is: when the sky splits open, etc., you, O man, will meet your Lord.

Al-Farra' permitted that the answer to "idha" be His words "wa adhinat li-rabbiha," and that the waw is superfluous in the answer. Ibn al-Anbari rejected this, on the grounds that the Arabs do not insert the waw except when "idha" comes after "hatta," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿حَتّى إذا جاءُوها وفُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ (Surah al-Zumar 39:73), or after "lamma," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَلَمّا أسْلَما وتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ ونادَيْناهُ أنْ يا إبْراهِيمُ﴾ (Surah al-Saffat 37:103), and so on.

It has also been said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. One of them may be the occasion of revelation, or it may be considered from the outset.

Ibn al-Anbari rejected this, on the grounds that the Arabs do not insert the waw except when "idha" comes after "hatta," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿حَتّى إذا جاءُوها وفُتِحَتْ أبْوابُها﴾ (Surah al-Zumar 39:73), or after "lamma," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَلَمّا أسْلَما وتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ ونادَيْناهُ أنْ يا إبْراهِيمُ﴾ (Surah al-Saffat 37:103), and so on.

It has also been said: the answer is ﴿فَأمّا مَن أُوتِيَ كِتابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ﴾ (Surah al-Inshiqaq 84:7). This was attributed to al-Kisa'i, and Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas approved of it.

The address is to all people, so the "al-" in His words "al-insan" is for defining the genus, and it is for comprehensiveness, as the detail in His words ﴿فَأمّا مَن أُوتِيَ كِتابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ﴾ (Surah al-Inshiqaq 84:7) up to His words ﴿كانَ بِهِ بَصِيرًا﴾ (Surah al-Inshiqaq 84:15) indicates.

The primary intent of this is the warning to the polytheists, because they are those who denied the resurrection, so the address regarding them is an added warning; and regarding the believers it is a reminder and good tidings. It has also been said: a specific person is intended, and it was said that he is al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad, with the unpointed sin in al-Isti'ab and al-Isabah, but in al-Kashshaf it occurs with the pointed shin, as al-Tibi vocalized it, and he said it is with the unpointed letter in Jami' al-Usul. It has also been said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. One of them may be the occasion of revelation, or it may be considered from the outset.

"Al-kadh" is applied to many meanings, the true reality of which we do not verify, and this root has been omitted in al-Asas, perhaps because the literal meaning was not established. The apparent statement of al-Raghib is that its reality is: exhausting oneself in work and toil. Attaching its prepositional complement in this verse with the particle "ila" indicates that the intended meaning is an action that ends in meeting God, so "kadih" may be taken as implying the sense of "sa'in" (striving), because people's toil in life seeks through today's work the work of tomorrow, and so on; likewise, the lifespan, which is the term of each person's life, passes with it, and it is followed by death, which is the return of the human soul to the pure disposal of God. When his striving and toil ended in death, his toil was made toward his Lord. So it is as if it were said: you are toiling, striving toward death, which is the meeting with your Lord. On this basis, the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial complement, a second predicate of "inna." It is also permissible that "kadih" be taken as implying the sense of "mashin" (walking), in which case the prepositional phrase is a loose (laghw) adverbial complement.

"Kadhan" is in the accusative as an absolute object to emphasize "kadih," taken as implying "sa'in ila rabbika," meaning: striving toward Him without doubt and without escape.

The pronoun of the object in "mulaqihi" refers to the Lord, meaning: "fa-mulaqin rabbaka," i.e., there is no escape for you from meeting God, and for this reason the predicate was emphasized with "inna."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 84, verses 1–6:

[218] ﴿When the sky splits open,﴾ ﴿and listens to its Lord, and it is worthy of that;﴾ ﴿and when the earth is stretched out,﴾ ﴿and casts out what is within it and empties itself,﴾ ﴿and listens to its Lord, and it is worthy of that;﴾ ﴿O man, you are toiling towards your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him.﴾

The adverbial phrase ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ (idha al-sama'u inshaqqat, "when the sky splits open") is placed before its governing verb, "kadih" (toiling), for the sake of awe-inspiring emphasis and to create suspense before the predicate. The original order of the speech in consideration is: "O man, you are toiling, when the sky splits open, etc."

However, since "idha" is attached to a part of the clause ﴿إنَّكَ كادِحٌ﴾ (innaka kadih, "you are toiling"), and since "idha" is an adverb carrying the meaning of a conditional, the sentence becomes: "O man, you are toiling" as the answer to the condition of "idha." Accordingly, they say that "idha" is an adverb that governs (khafid) its condition and is governed in the accusative (mansub) by its answer. That is, it governs the clause of its condition by being prefixed to it, and it is in the accusative by its answer, because it is connected to it. Thus both are governing and governed, according to the difference of perspective.

"Idha" is an adverb of future time, and the verb in the clause annexed to "idha" is interpreted as future, yet it is expressed in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, because the basic meaning of "idha" is the certainty of the condition's occurrence.

"Inshaqqat" is the intransitive (mutawi') form of "shaqqaha," meaning: when a splitter splits the sky, it splits; that is, God wills its splitting and it splits, as indicated by His following words, "and listens to its Lord."

"Al-inshiqaq" (splitting) here is the same as "al-infitar" mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْفَطَرَتْ﴾ (Surah al-Infitar 82:1). It is a splitting that appears to people in the atmosphere of the sky, due to a disruption in the composition of the air sphere, or due to the appearance of celestial bodies that leave their usual orbits in the upper atmosphere, so the air dome splits. It is thus a splitting that occurs when the order of this world is disrupted.

The subject is placed before the predicate verb in ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ rather than saying "idha inshaqqat al-sama'" in order to convey the strengthening of the judgment, which is the conditional suspension; that is, this condition is certain to occur, in addition to what the conditional "idha" implies of intending certainty of the occurrence of the condition, unlike "inna."

"Adhinat" means "istama'at" (listened). The verb "adhina" is derived from a fixed noun, which is the noun "udhun" (with a dammah on the hamza), the organ of hearing in a human. One says "udhun lahu," just as one says "istama' lahu," meaning he gave his ear to him.

[219] Here it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) in the sense of being affected: by God's creative command that it should split. It is not a metaphorical extension (isti'arah tab'iyyah) nor a representative metaphor (tamthiliyyah).

The expression "Rabbiha" (its Lord) is used instead of other divine names and ways of designating Him, because of what the description of the Lord implies of sovereignty and governance.

The clause "wa huqqat" is a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined clause and the clause it is conjoined to.

The meaning is: it is worthy of listening to its Lord, because it does not go outside the authority of His power, however great its thickness, however firm its creation, and however long the time of its sealing. All of that is only by God's decree for it; He is the one who, when He wills, removes it.

The object of "huqqat" is omitted, indicated by the verb "adhinat li-rabbiha," i.e., "and it is worthy of that submission and being affected." One says "huqqa fulanun bi-kadha," meaning a right was directed toward him. Since the agent of directing the right is generally not clear, the verb "huqqa bi-kadha" is used in the passive in usage, and its subject has the sense of the passive participle. So one says "haqiqun 'alayhi kadha" as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿حَقِيقٌ عَلى أنْ لا أقُولَ عَلى اللَّهِ إلّا الحَقَّ﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:105), and "huwa mahquq bi-kadha." Al-A'sha said:

"Indeed, you are worthy that you respond to his voice, and that you know that the one who is helped is successful."

The discussion of the clause ﴿وإذا الأرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾ (wa idha al-ardu muddat) is like the discussion of the clause ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ﴾ in placing the subject before the predicate verb.

"Madd al-ard" means spreading it out. The apparent meaning of this is that what is upon it of mountains is removed, as hide is stretched, so its folds disappear, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿ويَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الجِبالِ فَقُلْ يَنْسِفُها رَبِّي نَسْفًا فَيَذَرُها قاعًا صَفْصَفًا لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا ولا أمْتًا﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha 20:105).

[220] Among the meanings of "madd" is that it results from the expansion of the extent of its surface, by its cracking through earthquakes and the emergence of parts of its interior to its surface.

Among the meanings of "madd" is that its sphericity is removed by the stretching of its body until it becomes elongated after being round. All of that indicates the disruption of the order of the earth's movement and the change of the conditions of gravity and of the air sphere around the earth, and this is followed by the cessation of this world.

His words ﴿وألْقَتْ ما فِيها﴾ (and it casts out what is within it) are suitable to be understood in accordance with what fits these possibilities regarding the stretching of the earth, and they admit of the meaning that other parts are ejected from the interior of the earth, whose ejection has an effect in destroying existing things, such as volcanoes, the eruption of huge rocks, and the bursting forth of springs onto the surface of the earth, so that there is a flood.

"Takhallat" means it brought out what was in its interior so that nothing of it remained; because the verb "takhalla" indicates the intensity of emptying oneself of something, due to what the morphological pattern "tafa''ala" conveys of the sense of effort in the act, as one says "takarrama fulanun" when he exaggerated in generosity.

The meaning is: nothing remains of what is in the interior of the earth, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿وأخْرَجَتِ الأرْضُ أثْقالَها﴾ (Surah al-Zalzalah 99:2).

The discussion of the parallel of His words "wa adhinat li-rabbiha wa huqqat" has been mentioned above.

This was attributed to al-Mubarrad, meaning: because the last conjoined clause with "fa" in the reports is the one intended, of what was mentioned together with it.

So the meaning is: when the sky splits open and when the earth is stretched out, you will meet your Lord, O man, after your toil toward meeting Him. Thus His words ﴿إنَّكَ كادِحٌ﴾ are an interjected insertion placed before the intended point, like a parenthetical remark.

Al-Mubarrad also permitted that the answer to "idha" be omitted, indicated by His words "fa-mulaqihi," and the estimate is: when the sky splits open, etc., you, O man, will meet your Lord.

The apparent statement of al-Raghib is that its reality is: exhausting oneself in work and toil. The pronoun of the object in "mulaqihi" refers to the Lord, meaning: "fa-mulaqin rabbaka," i.e., there is no escape for you from meeting God, and for this reason the predicate was emphasized with "inna."

[p. 223]

This is a detailed account of the general statement in His words: ﴿Indeed, you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. That is, all people return to Allah. Whoever is given his record in his right hand is one group of people, namely the believers. Whoever is given his record behind his back is another group, namely the polytheists, as indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he thought he would never return﴾. Between these two ends there are degrees. This verse came in view of the division of people on that Day into the pious and the polytheists.

Al-kitab (the record) means the book of deeds. Being given it in the right hand was made a sign of happiness, because it is well known that the right hand takes up pure things. This is rooted in human nature, arising from the fact that the right side of the body is stronger and more ready for the action that the will is set on doing. Thus it became fixed in souls that blessing lies on the right side, to the point that they called blessing and happiness "yumn" (right-hand fortune), and they labeled its opposite with ill omen. So the blessing of the right hand is among what Allah, Exalted is He, placed in the original nature of man. This was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right"﴾ [al-Saffat: 28] in Surat al-Saffat, and at His words: ﴿And the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27], and His words: ﴿And the companions of the left—what are the companions of the left?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 41], and His words: ﴿So the companions of the right—what are the companions of the right? And the companions of the left—what are the companions of the left?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8] in Surat al-Waqi'ah.

The "ba'" in His words "bi-yaminihi" (in his right hand) is for accompaniment or association, or it means "fi" (in), and it is connected to "utiya" (was given).

The particle sawfa originally indicates that an action will occur in the future. Most often it is meant to refer to the distant future, and that is the common usage. In eloquent usage, it is intended to affirm that the action will certainly occur and continue. An example is His words: ﴿He said, "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf: 98] in Surat Yusuf. Here it conveys certainty and continuity with respect to an action that is capable of continuity, which is "yanqalibu ila ahlihi masrurًا" (he returns to his family joyful). This is the purpose of this promise. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿We will surely cause him to burn in fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 30] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The easy reckoning (al-hisab al-yasir) is the presentation of his deeds to him without dispute, so its duration is not long, and he is quickly brought to Paradise. This applies when his deeds are righteous. Thus "easy reckoning" is a kinayah (metonymy) for the absence of censure.

And "the one who is given his record behind his back" is the disbeliever. The meaning is that his record is given to him in his left hand, as the contrast with "the one who is given his record in his right hand" requires. This is also indicated in Surat al-Haqqah, in His words: ﴿But as for he who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record"﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25]. That is, his record is given to him from behind, and he takes it in his left hand, as a way of belittling him. It is handed to him from behind his back to show anger toward him, such that the one who hands him the record does not look at his face.

The adverbial phrase "behind his back" is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) for "his record."

﴿Yanqalibu ila ahlihi﴾ means he returns. Inqilab (returning) is going back to the place from which one came. It was discussed shortly before in Surat al-Mutaffifin.

Al-ahl means the household: wife, children, and kin.

This expression is a figurative image (tamthil) of the state of one who is reckoned with an easy reckoning, in joy, success, and salvation after righteous deeds in this world. It is likened to the state of a traveler on a trade journey who returns to his family safe and profitable, because of the abundance of joy in the image that is compared: success, profit, safety, and meeting one's family, all of them rejoicing. This is the point of resemblance between the two states, namely the joy familiar to the audience. So the statement is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah).

The intended meaning is not his return to his dwelling in Paradise, because he did not have a dwelling there before, so that his arrival there could be called a return. Also, he may not have a family there. It is also a kinayah for the length of rest, because a traveler who returns to his family leaves hardship behind for a time.

[p. 224]

The word "du'a'" in His words ﴿yad'u thubura﴾ (he calls out for destruction) means calling out, that is, he cries out "thubur," saying, "O my destruction," or "O destruction," just as one says, "O woe is me" and "O our woe."

Thubur means ruin and bad condition. It is a word said by one who has fallen into misery and wretchedness.

The calling out in words like these is used to express lamentation and anguish, from the meaning of the noun that follows the vocative particle.

As for "sayuslha" (he will burn), Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and al-Kisa'i read it with a doubled lam, from the verb salla, which means to burn it. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, Abu Ja'far, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it as yaslaa, with a fatha on the yaa' and a light lam, the imperfect of the intransitive saliya, meaning to be touched by fire, as in His words: ﴿They will burn in it on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Infitar: 15].

The word sa'ran (blazing fire) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, with the sense of "yaslaa bi-sa'ir" (he will burn in a blazing fire). This is the aspect that applies consistently in all places where the word for fire or similar appears in the accusative after verbs derived from salaa and tasliyah (burning). We already presented this aspect in explaining His words: ﴿And they will soon taste the blazing fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 10] in Surat al-Nisa'. Refer to it there.

His words: ﴿Indeed, he was among his family, joyful﴾ are used for expressing wonder at their state: how they turned from that joy they had in the worldly life, known from their conditions described in many verses, such as His words: ﴿Those of luxury﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and His words: ﴿And when they returned to their families, they returned jesting﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 31]. Then they came to the pain of the Fire in the Hereafter, to the point that they called out for destruction.

Emphasizing the report is a feature of reports used for expressing wonder, like the saying of 'Umar to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman: "Indeed, you are bold toward him," meaning toward the Prophet (ﷺ).

This sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah).

The position of the sentence ﴿Indeed, he thought he would never return﴾ is that of a causal explanation for the content of the sentence ﴿But as for he who is given his record behind his back﴾ to its end.

The particle inna in it replaces the causal fa'. So the meaning is: "He will burn in a blazing fire because he thought he would never return," that is, he would never return to life after death, that is, because he denies the resurrection. It is said: "Ha'ara yahuru" when one returns to the place where he was. Then it was applied to returning to a state one was in after leaving it, and this is what is meant here. It is one of the common figurative usages in applying "return" to it, as in His words: ﴿Then to Us is your return﴾ [Yunus: 23], and His words: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8]. The Day of Resurrection is called the Day of Return (ma'ad).

The particle lan is used, which indicates emphasis and perpetuity of negation, to convey their firm and definite conviction in denying it.

The particle bala is used to answer a negative statement in order to nullify its negation. Most often it follows a question that asks about a negation, as in His words: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes (bala)"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. It also occurs after non-interrogative statements, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, "Yes (bala), by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected"﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7].

The position of bala is that of a new sentence (isti'naf), like the particles of response.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾ explains in summary the nullification conveyed by the particle bala. That is, his thought is false, because his Lord informed him that he would be resurrected.

The meaning is: Indeed, his Lord is knowing of his end. The emphasis with inna is to refute his denial of the resurrection, which Allah reported through His Messenger (ﷺ). So the meaning arising from the particle of nullification and the particle of emphasis comes to mean: His Lord is seeing of him, while he himself is not seeing of his own condition, like His words: ﴿Allah knows, and you do not know﴾.

The transitive use of başîran with the preposition bi- is because it derives from basura (intransitive, with a damma on the sad), meaning to see it with a clear and certain sight. So the bi- in it means association or attachment.

In this is an indication of the wisdom of resurrection for requital, because the Lord of people has knowledge of their conditions. Among them are the reformer and the corrupter, and all differ in this. So it is not wise that the corrupter should go with his corruption and the harms he has inflicted on existing things, while the reformer's righteousness is neglected. So Allah made life eternal and made it for requital for what its owner put forward in his first life.

The word "basar" (sight) here is used for complete knowledge of a thing.

The description "basir" is connected to the pronoun of the human being who thought he would never return. The meaning is knowledge of his conditions, not of his essence.

Placing the prepositional phrase before what it governs is for emphasis on this prepositional phrase, that is: "He is surely seeing of him," while observing the rhyme endings (fawasil).

The *fa'* (ف) here marks the consequence of the oath and its answer, following on from the detailed account in His words ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 7) up to this point. This implies that there is a reckoning and a recompense for good and evil. So this consequence serves as a summary and conclusion of the states that have been detailed. It is also a general gathering of the terrors that arise in that process.

It has been mentioned that *lā uqsimu* ("I do not swear") means *uqsimu* ("I swear"), and the reason for swearing by these states and created things was explained at His words ﴿So I swear by the stars that recede﴾ (At-Takwir: 15) in Surat At-Takwir.

The connection between the things sworn by here and what is sworn to is that twilight, night and the moon pass through states that lie between darkness and the appearance of light, or within them. This fits His words ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage﴾, with its variation of states in which people are tossed about on the Day of Resurrection, or in their worldly life. Or it may refer to the appearance of good states amid evil ones, or to waiting for states to change into what pleases them, if the address is to the believers specifically, as will come later.

Perhaps the mention of twilight hints that it resembles the state at the end of the world, since the setting of the sun is like the state of death. The mention of night hints at the intensity of the terror on the Day of Reckoning, and the mention of the moon hints at the attainment of mercy by the believers.

*Al-shafaq* (twilight): the name for the redness that appears on the horizon of the west after the sun sets. It is a light from the rays of the sun when some part of the body of the earth screens it from people's eyes. There is disagreement over whether the whiteness that follows the redness is also called *shafaq*.

**[p. 227 continued]**

*Wa mā wasaq* (and what it gathers): *mā* here may be a verbal-source particle (meaning "and the gathering of..."), or it may be a relative pronoun ("and what it gathers"), in the manner of the omitted accusative returning pronoun.

*Al-wasq*: gathering things, one upon another. The meaning may be what is gathered of things that were scattered during the day, of people and animals, for they return to their shelters at night. This is part of the natural disposition that God placed in living beings, seeking rest at night. He said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (Al-Qasas: 73). This is one of the wonders of creation, and for this reason He swore by it, making a favour part of the oath.

It has also been said that what the night gathers is the stars, because they appear at night. Their appearance in it is likened to the gatherer gathering scattered things. This fits better with the conjunction of the moon to it.

*Ittisaq* of the moon (its gathering): the gathering of its light. It is an *ifti'al* form from *al-wasq* in the sense of gathering, as mentioned just before. This occurs on the night of the full moon. Restricting the oath to that state is because it is the manifestation of God's blessing upon people through its light.

The root of the verb *ittasaqa* is *awtasaqa*: the *waw* was changed into a *ta'* to facilitate its assimilation into the *ta'* of the *ifti'al* form. This is a regular change.

The clause ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ has its wording woven in a concise way, to gather the many meanings that the listeners' minds may reach. It came in the most excellent form of composition for speech that is sent forth as proverbs: concise, marvellously woven, and rich in meaning. For this reason the interpreters' explanations of it are many.

The figurative meanings of *riding*, and the literal and figurative meanings of *ṭabaq* (stage/layer), give latitude for the meanings the verse conveys. This is what gave the choice of these two words in this verse a particular quality among the branches of the Qur'anic inimitability.

As for the verb *latarkabunna* (you will surely ride), its literal meaning is impossible here. It has several figurative meanings used in speech, or which may be intended in the verse: overcoming, following, travelling along a path, entering upon something, persisting in, and rising high.

**[p. 228]**

The origin of these meanings is either a metaphor (*isti'āra*) or a figure of speech (*tamthīl*). It is said: "He rode a difficult matter" and "he committed (rode) an error."

As for the word *ṭabaq*, its literal meaning is a singular noun for a thing equal to another thing in its size and measure. The apparent statement of the lexicons *al-Asās* and *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* is that equality with the qualifier that the *ṭabaq* is higher than what it equals makes it literal for a cover. So it belongs among words coined for a restricted meaning, like *khiwān* (table) and *ka's* (cup). The apparent statement of *al-Kashshāf* is that its literal meaning is absolute equality, so the qualifier of being raised high is incidental due to the predominance of usage. It is said: "The sandal matched the sandal" (*ṭābaqa al-na'l al-na'l*).

Whichever is the case, it is a noun on the pattern *faʿal*. It is either derived from *al-muṭābaqa* (matching), like the derivation of the resembling adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), and then treated as a noun, the derivation being forgotten. Or its origin is the noun *al-ṭabaq*, meaning a cover, which was considered in a comparison and then forgotten; the root *ṭ-b-q* in the sense of equality then came from it. In that case it is among derived forms from non-derived nouns.

It is also used as a singular noun for the cover with which something is covered. From this is the proverb: "The waterskin matched its cover" (*wāfaqa shannun ṭabaqata*), meaning its lid. This is literal, because a cover is equal to what it covers. *Ṭabaq* is also used for a state, because it attaches to its possessor as a cover attaches to what it covers.

It is also used as a singular noun for an object made of leather or wood, on which food is eaten and in which fruits and the like are placed. It was apparently called *ṭabaq* because its origin is to be used as a cover for vessels, and things are placed in it.

It is also used as a collective noun for *ṭabaqa*, which is a place above another place of similar measure, but raised above it. This is metaphorical. One says: "A *ṭabaq* of people came to us," meaning a group.

The difference in the meanings of the two words is accompanied by the difference in the meaning of *ʿan* (from): either the literal meaning of passing beyond (*mujāwaza*), or the figurative meaning of being synonymous with *baʿda* (after).

Likewise, the difference in the grammatical reading of *ṭabaqan* as an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) or as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). These possibilities increase if the sentences are not restricted to what has a connection with the context of the speech, from the place of the sentence after the verse ﴿O man, you are toiling toward your Lord﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 6) and so on. And from its occurring after the oath, which suggests emphasis, and from the imperfect verb after the oath implying the future. Thus many meanings can be composed from these possibilities, fit to explain the verse.

Perhaps the mention of twilight hints that it resembles the state at the end of the world, since the setting of the sun is like the state of death. The mention of night hints at the intensity of the terror on the Day of Reckoning, and the mention of the moon hints at the attainment of mercy by the believers.

*Al-shafaq* (twilight): the name for the redness that appears on the horizon of the west after the sun sets. It is a light from the rays of the sun when some part of the body of the earth screens it from people's eyes. There is disagreement over whether the whiteness that follows the redness is also called *shafaq*.

**[p. 227 continued]**

*Wa mā wasaq* (and what it gathers): *mā* here may be a verbal-source particle (meaning "and the gathering of..."), or it may be a relative pronoun ("and what it gathers"), in the manner of the omitted accusative returning pronoun.

*Al-wasq*: gathering things, one upon another. The meaning may be what is gathered of things that were scattered during the day, of people and animals, for they return to their shelters at night. This is part of the natural disposition that God placed in living beings, seeking rest at night. He said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (Al-Qasas: 73). This is one of the wonders of creation, and for this reason He swore by it, making a favour part of the oath.

It has also been said that what the night gathers is the stars, because they appear at night. Their appearance in it is likened to the gatherer gathering scattered things. This fits better with the conjunction of the moon to it.

*Ittisaq* of the moon (its gathering): the gathering of its light. It is an *ifti'al* form from *al-wasq* in the sense of gathering, as mentioned just before. This occurs on the night of the full moon. Restricting the oath to that state is because it is the manifestation of God's blessing upon people through its light.

The root of the verb *ittasaqa* is *awtasaqa*: the *waw* was changed into a *ta'* to facilitate its assimilation into the *ta'* of the *ifti'al* form. This is a regular change.

The clause ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ has its wording woven in a concise way, to gather the many meanings that the listeners' minds may reach. It came in the most excellent form of composition for speech that is sent forth as proverbs: concise, marvellously woven, and rich in meaning. For this reason the interpreters' explanations of it are many.

The figurative meanings of *riding*, and the literal and figurative meanings of *ṭabaq* (stage/layer), give latitude for the meanings the verse conveys. This is what gave the choice of these two words in this verse a particular quality among the branches of the Qur'anic inimitability.

As for the verb *latarkabunna* (you will surely ride), its literal meaning is impossible here. It has several figurative meanings used in speech, or which may be intended in the verse: overcoming, following, travelling along a path, entering upon something, persisting in, and rising high.

**[p. 228]**

The origin of these meanings is either a metaphor (*isti'āra*) or a figure of speech (*tamthīl*). It is said: "He rode a difficult matter" and "he committed (rode) an error."

As for the word *ṭabaq*, its literal meaning is a singular noun for a thing equal to another thing in its size and measure. The apparent statement of the lexicons *al-Asās* and *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* is that equality with the qualifier that the *ṭabaq* is higher than what it equals makes it literal for a cover. So it belongs among words coined for a restricted meaning, like *khiwān* (table) and *ka's* (cup). The apparent statement of *al-Kashshāf* is that its literal meaning is absolute equality, so the qualifier of being raised high is incidental due to the predominance of usage. It is said: "The sandal matched the sandal" (*ṭābaqa al-na'l al-na'l*).

Whichever is the case, it is a noun on the pattern *faʿal*. It is either derived from *al-muṭābaqa* (matching), like the derivation of the resembling adjective (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), and then treated as a noun, the derivation being forgotten. Or its origin is the noun *al-ṭabaq*, meaning a cover, which was considered in a comparison and then forgotten; the root *ṭ-b-q* in the sense of equality then came from it. In that case it is among derived forms from non-derived nouns.

It is also used as a singular noun for the cover with which something is covered. From this is the proverb: "The waterskin matched its cover" (*wāfaqa shannun ṭabaqata*), meaning its lid. This is literal, because a cover is equal to what it covers. *Ṭabaq* is also used for a state, because it attaches to its possessor as a cover attaches to what it covers.

It is also used as a singular noun for an object made of leather or wood, on which food is eaten and in which fruits and the like are placed. It was apparently called *ṭabaq* because its origin is to be used as a cover for vessels, and things are placed in it.

It is also used as a collective noun for *ṭabaqa*, which is a place above another place of similar measure, but raised above it. This is metaphorical. One says: "A *ṭabaq* of people came to us," meaning a group.

The difference in the meanings of the two words is accompanied by the difference in the meaning of *ʿan* (from): either the literal meaning of passing beyond (*mujāwaza*), or the figurative meaning of being synonymous with *baʿda* (after).

Likewise, the difference in the grammatical reading of *ṭabaqan* as an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) or as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). These possibilities increase if the sentences are not restricted to what has a connection with the context of the speech, from the place of the sentence after the verse ﴿O man, you are toiling toward your Lord﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 6) and so on. And from its occurring after the oath, which suggests emphasis, and from the imperfect verb after the oath implying the future. Thus many meanings can be composed from these possibilities, fit to explain the verse.

It was said that the meaning is: "You will surely ride one state after another." This was transmitted by al-Bukhari from Ibn ʿAbbas from the Prophet (ﷺ). The more apparent view is that it is a warning of the terrors of the Resurrection. The *tanwīn* (nunation) of *ṭabaq* in both places is for magnification and awe. *ʿAn* has the meaning of *baʿda* (after), and the sense of "after" here is a relative one: a progression of after, meaning: "you will surely encounter a terror greater than a terror", like His words ﴿We will add to them punishment upon punishment﴾ (An-Nahl: 88). Using *ṭabaq* for a state on this interpretation is because the state corresponds to the work of its possessor.

Abu Nuʿaym transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah an explanation of the states as states of death and life, of resurrection, of happiness or wretchedness, of bliss or the Fire, as God writes for each person at the time of his creation. Jabir transmitted this from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Kathir said: "This is a rejected (*munkar*) hadith, and its chain contains weak narrators."

Or it means one state after another of the hardships of the Resurrection. This was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima and al-Hasan, with differences in specifying the states.

It was also said: "You will surely ride one station after another", on the basis that *ṭabaq* is the name of a station. This was transmitted from Ibn Zayd and Saʿid ibn Jubayr. That is: "You will surely pass from the stage of this world to the stage of the Hereafter." Or: some people were humble in this world and were exalted in the Hereafter. In that case the *tanwīn* is for the sequence (*tafrī*).

It was also said: whoever is upon righteousness is called by it to another righteousness, and whoever is upon corruption is called by it to a corruption above it, because everything draws towards its own kind. In that case the sentence is an interjection of admonition, and *ʿan* in this view is in its literal sense of passing beyond. The *tanwīn* is for magnification.

It is possible that riding is a metaphor for travelling, by the relation of the general to the particular: "You will surely be brought to the Reckoning in groups after groups," in the sense of His words ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the driving﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 30). This is a threat to those who deny. So riding is used for following, meaning: "you will surely follow one another." The object of *latarkabunna* is omitted, with the implied meaning: "that some of you will follow others" in your insistence on denying the Resurrection. The evidence for the omitted object is His words ﴿stage after stage﴾. *Ṭabaqan* would then be an object, and its accusative is either as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *latarkabunna*, or as an object, according to what suits the meanings of the words of the verse.

**[p. 230]**

The position of ﴿from stage to stage﴾ (*ʿan ṭabaqin*) is that of a qualifier for *ṭabaqan*.

The meaning of *ʿan* is either figurative, or it is synonymous with *baʿda* (after). The latter is a metaphor arising from the meaning of passing beyond. For this reason the poet Al-Nabigha altered the phrase of those who said "they inherited glory, elder from elder" (*wirithū al-majd kābiran ʿan kābirin*), changing the preposition *ʿan* to the word *baʿda*, and said:

*For the house of Al-Jilah, elder after elder.*

Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿĀṣim and Abu Jaʿfar read *latarkabunna* with a *ḍamma* on the *bāʾ*, as an address to people. The others read it with a *fatḥa* on the *bāʾ*, as an address to man, from His words ﴿O man, you are toiling toward your Lord﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 6). It is also taken to mean that the *ta'* is the feminine third-person prefix, and the pronoun returns to the heaven: states succeed one another for it, of splitting asunder, folding up, and at one time being like oil dregs and at another like molten brass. It was said: it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it was said that it is a promise of victory, meaning: "you will surely take charge of the affairs of the Arabs tribe after tribe, and conquest after conquest," as occurred after that, that is, after the revelation of the verse, when the strength of the Muslims grew. So it is good news for the Muslims. The sentence then comes as an interjection with *fa'*, between the sentence ﴿He thought that he would never return﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 14) and the sentence ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 20). This view works with both readings.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate.﴾

It is possible that this is a consequence of what was mentioned about the state of the one who is given his record behind his back, and the plural pronoun refers back to him, because what is meant by the relative "man" (*man*) is every person to whom the relative clause applies, so the pronoun follows the sense of *man*, which is plural. The meaning is: "What is wrong with them that they do not fear the terrors of the Day of meeting Allah, so that they would believe?"

It is also possible that this is a consequence of His saying: ﴿O mankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. That is: once you have come to know this, how can those who denied the Resurrection not believe in it?! The pronoun of the third person is used because the intended object of the denial and wonder is specifically the polytheists among those whom the word "mankind" (*al-insan*) included in His saying: ﴿O mankind, you are toiling﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6], because concern for admonishing them is more important. So the pronoun is an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person).

It is also possible that it is a consequence of His saying: ﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19], so that it is specific to the polytheists on the basis that they are the most in need of these admonitions. The pronoun is also an *iltifat*.

It is also possible that it is a consequence of what the oath includes of the states of the things sworn by, on the basis that the swearing by them implies that they are signs of the great power of Allah, the Exalted, and of His singularity in divinity. So mentioning them is a reminder, by their indication of the Oneness (of Allah). The *iltifat* is the same.

The construction ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ contains the interrogative *ma*, which is the subject of the predicate expressed by the prepositional phrase *lahum* (to them, for them), and the clause after *lahum* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the interrogative *ma*.

This interrogation is used to express wonder at their failure to believe and to deny that their not believing is justified, because the nature of a strange and reprehensible matter is that one asks about it. So using the interrogative to mean wonder and denial is a metaphor (*majaz*) by the relation of necessary consequence (*'alaqat al-luzum*), and the *lam* is for specification (*li-l-ikhtisas*).

The clause ﴿do not believe﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), for if a noun had occupied its place it would have been in the accusative, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with you regarding the hypocrites, that you are two groups?﴾ [an-Nisa': 88]. The circumstantial clause is the focus of the wonder. The detailed discussion of its construction and of the forms in which similar constructions occur has already been presented at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "And what is wrong with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The object of *yu'minun* (believe) is omitted, and the context indicates it, that is: in the Resurrection and the recompense.

It is also possible to treat the verb *yu'minun* as intransitive (*manzilat al-lazim*), that is: they do not characterize themselves with faith; that is, what is the cause of their not being believers, given the manifest signs indicating the singularity of Allah, the Exalted, in divinity? So how can they persist in associating others with Him?!

The meaning: wonder and denial at their failure to believe, despite the manifest proofs of the truth of what they were called to and warned about.

﴿Do not prostrate﴾ is coordinated with ﴿do not believe﴾, and ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them﴾ is an adverbial phrase (*zarf*) placed before its governing verb for the sake of emphasis on it and to highlight the status of the Qur'an.

The recitation of the Qur'an to them is its recitation as a means of conveying the message and of call, and the Prophet ﷺ used to present the Qur'an to them in groups and individually. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said to him: "Do not trouble us with it in our gatherings." The Prophet ﷺ also recited the Qur'an to al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, as we mentioned in Surat 'Abasa.

Prostration (*sujud*) is used with the meaning of submission and humility, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [ar-Rahman: 6], and His saying: ﴿Its shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah﴾ [an-Nahl: 48]. That is: when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not submit to Allah, or to the meanings and proof of the Qur'an, and they do not believe in its reality. The evidence for this meaning is its contrast with His saying: (﴿Rather, those who disbelieved deny﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 22]).

There is nothing in this verse that requires that there is a prostration of Qur'anic recitation (*sajdat al-Qur'an*) at this verse. The more correct view of Malik and his companions is that it is not one of the prostrations of the Qur'an, contrary to Ibn Wahb, one of Malik's companions, who counted the prostrations of the Qur'an as fourteen. Al-Shafi'i said: it is a *sunnah* (recommended). Abu Hanifah said: it is obligatory (*wajibah*). The more preferred view is that the prostrations that are attributed as the obligatory prostrations (*'aza'im al-sujud*) are eleven prostrations, and these are the ones transmitted through authentic chains from the Companions. As for three verses beyond the eleven, reports exist that the Prophet ﷺ prostrated when reciting them, and among them is this one; but other reports contradict them, so either he left their prostration or he did not emphasize it. Among them is His saying, exalted is He, here: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The prostration in Surat al-Inshiqaq is the view of the Madinan companions of Malik." End of quotation.

I say: this is the view of Ibn Wahb, and there is no special status for this verse; rather, it concerns the three extra prostrations beyond the eleven. Malik said in the *Muwatta'*, after narrating the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "The matter among us is that the obligatory prostrations are eleven prostrations, and there is none of them in the *mufassal* (the final, short surahs of the Qur'an)." Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: the prostrations of recitation are fourteen, with the addition of the prostration of Surat an-Najm, the prostration of Surat al-Inshiqaq, and the prostration of Surat al-'Alaq. Ahmad said: they are fifteen prostrations, with the addition of the prostration at the end of the verse in Surat al-Hajj, so there are two prostrations in it according to him.

﴿Nay, those who disbelieve deny.﴾

It is possible that *bal* here is an *idrab intiqali* (a transitional shift, a change of direction in the discourse) away from expressing wonder at their failure to believe and rebuking them for it, toward informing about them that they persist in disbelief and in attacking the Qur'an. The speech then ascends in its wonder and rebuke.

The informing about them that they "deny" is used to express wonder and rebuke. For this reason it is expressed with the present tense verb, which conveys the sense of the state being present before the mind, as in His saying: ﴿He argues with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ (Hud: 74).

It is also possible that *bal* is an *idrab ibtali* (a shift that negates what precedes it), meaning: there is no cause for which they do not believe or do not affirm the Qur'an. Rather, the reality is the opposite of that, for the motives to belief from the proofs are abundant, and the reasons for acknowledging the truthfulness of the Qur'an and submitting to its call are manifest, yet they deny. That is, they persist in denial out of obstinacy and arrogance. His saying indicates this: ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾ (al-Inshiqaq: 23).

These two meanings are parallel to the two aspects in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Infitar: ﴿Nay, you deny the Judgment﴾ (al-Infitar: 9) ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ (al-Infitar: 10).

The use of the present tense verb indicates that the denial occurs from them and is renewed. That is: rather, they persist in denial out of obstinacy, and this is not from belief. Just as the renewal of faith and the renewal of submission at the recitation of the Qur'an are negated of them, so the renewal of denial is affirmed for them.

His saying *alladhina kafaru* ("those who disbelieve") is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun. The expected form would have been "Nay, they deny," but it was changed to the relative pronoun and its clause, because of what the clause implies of condemning them with disbelief, to point to the cause of the statement. That is: they persisted in denial because disbelief is rooted in them and they are characterized by it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 84, verse 23:

﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.﴾

This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD) placed between the clause ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 22] and the clause ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24]. It is a metaphorical expression (kinaya) for warning and threat, meaning that Allah will requite them for the evil of their inner intentions.

Page 234

The meaning of ﴿what they conceal﴾ (bi-ma yu'un) is what they hide in their hearts of obstinacy, while they know that what the Qur'an has brought is true, but they openly display denial of it so that their turning away from it will be accepted by their followers and their neighbours.

The original meaning of al-iya' (إيعاء) is making something a container (wi'a'), and the wi'a' (وِعاء), with a kasra on the waw, is a receptacle, because things are gathered into it. Then its use spread to the gathering of things so that they would not be lost, and so it came to carry the sense of hoarding (taqtir). From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And he gathered and hoarded﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 18]. And in the hadith: "Do not hoard, lest Allah hoard (withhold) from you." It is used in this verse with the meaning of concealment, because hoarding (iya') necessarily entails concealment; thus it is here a metonymy (majaz mursal).

This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve deny it﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 22].

The verb "bashshirhum" (﴿give them good tidings﴾) is used metaphorically (isti'arah) to mean warning and threat, in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum). The reason is that the real meaning of "tabshir" (giving good tidings) is informing of what delights and benefits. But when the phrase "a painful punishment" is attached to the verb, the indication of sarcasm (qarinah) becomes like a fire upon a landmark. This is of the same kind as the words of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you, then hastened your hospitality
before dawn, with a grinding millstone-like club."

Verse 25 of Surat al-Inshiqaq: ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward that will never be cut off.﴾

It is permissible for the exception (istithna', exception clause) to be connected (muttasil), in one of two ways:

First, it may be an exception from the pronoun in His words ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19], following its interpretation as riding through the layers of hardships and terrors on the Day of Resurrection, and what is similar to that in threat.

Second, it may be an exception from the plural pronoun in "so give them good tidings" (fa-bashshirhum), and the meaning is: except those among those who are now polytheists who will believe, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except those who repent, make amends, and make things clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160], and His saying in Surat al-Buruj: ﴿Indeed, those who persecute the believing men and believing women and then do not repent...﴾ [al-Buruj: 10].

The verb "āmanū" (they believed) in this way is intended to refer to the future, and it is expressed in the past tense to draw attention to the meaning: those whose faith is established. What lies between this and His saying ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20] up to here is an interposed subsidiary clause between the excepted and the excepted-from, singled out for the most important of those included in the generality of ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19].

It has also been said: it is an exception that is disjunct (munqati', not from the same category) from the pronoun in "fa-bashshirhum", so it is included in the giving of good tidings, which is used in mockery, in order to increase the grief upon them. Thus the particle illa (except) has the function of "lakin" (but), and the adversative (istidrak) by it is merely for opposition, not to remove a suspicion that the opposite of that is intended. Similar to this is frequent in adversative usage. As for some scholars' definition of istidrak as "following a statement by removing what is assumed to be affirmed or negated," it is an approximate definition.

The clause ﴿for them is a reward that will never be cut off﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), as if a questioner asked: "What is their state on the day when those [people] are in painful punishment?" The reward that will never be cut off is that which its recipient is given together with honour, in such a way that it is not accompanied by a reproach, as His exalted saying indicated: ﴿as a recompense for what they used to do﴾ and similar to it, of what mentions the cause along with the recompense. The meaning is that their reward is a joy for them, unmixed with any trace of distress, for reproach spoils a favour. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. And al-Nabigha said:

"A favour for 'Amr upon me after favour, to his father; it is not one with scorpions."

Among the excellent sayings of the scholar al-Zamakhshari: "The taste of blessings is sweeter than reproach, and it is more bitter than blessings with reproach."

It is also permissible for "ghayr mamnun" to mean "ghayr maqtu'" (uncut, unbroken). It is said: "mananta al-habl" when you cut the rope. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and abundant fruit﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 32], ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 33].

Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, the Kharijite, asked 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas about His saying "ghayr mamnun", and he said: "Ghayr maqtu'" (uncut). He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes, the brother of Yashkur has known it," meaning al-Harith ibn Hilliza, where he says:

"Then you see behind them, from the speed of their return, a dust-cloud (maninan), as if it were fine dust."

Al-manin: the dust, because they cut it off behind them.

Surat al-Buruj

Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite in the late night prayer (al-'isha' al-akhirah) 'By the sky with its mansions' (al-sama' dhat al-buruj)." This is apparent that it is named "Surat al-sama' dhat al-buruj," because he did not relate the wording of the Qur'an, since he did not mention the wa (and).

Ahmad also narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded that the [two surahs] be recited in 'isha' by 'al-samawat'," meaning "al-sama' dhat al-buruj" and "al-sama' wa al-tariq," so he put them together in the plural form of sama'. This indicates that the names of the two surahs are: Surat al-sama' dhat al-buruj and Surat al-sama' wa al-tariq.

It is named in the mushafs, the books of Sunnah, and the books of tafsir "Surat al-Buruj."

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the twenty-seventh in the enumeration of the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Shams (wa al-shamsi wa duhaha) and Surat al-Tin.

Its number of verses is twenty-two.

The Aims of This Surah

The aims of this surah begin with a parable for those who persecuted the Muslims in Makkah: that they are like a people who persecuted a group of those who believed in God, and they made a trench of fire for their torment, so that the parable would be a strengthening for the Muslims, a means of patience for them against the harm of the polytheists, and a reminder of what befell their predecessors in faith of severe torment that had not touched them in its like, yet that did not turn them from their religion.

[Page 237]

And an assurance to the Muslims that the might of God is great, so the polytheists will meet the requital of their deeds, and the Muslims will attain eternal bliss and victory.

And an allusion to the Muslims regarding their honour with God, exalted is He.

A parable was struck with the people of Pharaoh and Thamud, and how the end of their affair was, since they denied the Messengers. Thus the lesson was achieved for the polytheists in their persecution of the Muslims and in their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), and in the exalting of the status of the Qur'an.
